Formulation
- Predisposing factors: History of childhood asthma and seasonal hay fever increase susceptibility to airway hyperreactivity.
- Precipitating factors: Recent house cleaning with dust exposure likely triggered acute respiratory symptoms.
- Perpetuating factors: Lack of immediate antihistamine at home; uncertain recent inhaler availability/use; increasing anxiety about breathing may worsen perception of symptoms.
- Protective factors: Patient has an inhaler (per report), is able and willing to attend in-person assessment at a clinic/GP (minutes' drive away), and sought care promptly.
- Summary: A 40-year-old patient with past childhood asthma and seasonal hay fever developed progressive wheeze and breathlessness following dust exposure. Symptoms worsen at night and impair speech. Plan focuses on rapid assessment to distinguish asthma exacerbation from allergic reaction and initiation of appropriate treatment.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Acute wheeze/shortness of breath (probable asthma exacerbation vs allergic reaction)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Relief of breathlessness and wheeze
  - Ability to speak without interruption
  - Receive prompt assessment and appropriate treatment
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Rapid in-person assessment to determine oxygenation and cause (asthma vs allergy)
  - Provide symptomatic treatment as indicated (antihistamine and/or corticosteroids and/or inhaler therapy)
  - Ensure follow-up with GP and update asthma management as needed
- Actions (Patient):
  - Attend an in-person clinic/GP appointment for assessment and testing (patient agreed)
  - Obtain and take an OTC antihistamine on the way to the clinic if available
  - Bring any current inhaler to the appointment and use as needed
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Perform in-person assessment including pulse oximetry (finger oximeter) and clinical respiratory exam
  - Consider prescribing or administering antihistamine and/or oral/inhaled steroids if indicated after assessment
  - Provide documentation/letter to the patient’s GP (letter to be sent via app as per consultation)
  - Arrange brief in-person consultation (~10 minutes estimated) and plan follow-up as needed

Secondary Problem: Chronic/previous asthma and seasonal hay fever
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Review and optimize asthma and allergy management to reduce future exacerbations
  - Ensure access to and understanding of inhaler use and action plan
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Confirm current inhaler regimen and adherence; update prescriptions if required
  - Review need for an asthma action plan and allergy management (including antihistamine use)
- Actions (Patient):
  - Present to GP with inhaler and history; discuss past steroid use and seasonal hay fever
  - Arrange follow-up review of asthma control with GP if recommended
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Review and, if necessary, prescribe inhaler therapy or a course of steroids
  - Provide or update an asthma action plan and advice on allergy prevention and medication
  - Document history of prior steroid use and consider in current management decisions

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Need for in-person assessment/tests (pulse oximetry) to distinguish asthma vs allergic cause
  - Use of an antihistamine for suspected allergy (OTC available) and potential need for steroids depending on assessment
  - Importance of attending GP/clinic promptly; expected short consultation duration
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - Increasing breathlessness
  - Difficulty speaking or completing sentences due to breathlessness
  - Progressive wheeze or overnight worsening
  - (Patient advised to seek assessment if symptoms continue/worsen)
- Coping Strategies:
  - Use inhaler as needed and bring it to appointments
  - Take OTC antihistamine if allergic trigger suspected
  - Attend in-person assessment promptly for objective monitoring (oxygen saturations) and treatment
